title: Python List Methods: count(), index() and reverse()
learningObjectives: Use list.count(value) to count occurrences of a value.
Use list.index(value, start, end) to locate the first matching value.
Handle ValueError when index() cannot find a value.
Use list.reverse() to reverse a list in place.
Distinguish reverse() from slicing and sorted() when choosing whether to mutate the original list.

understand.concept: Python lists provide count(value), index(value, start, end) and reverse(). count returns the number of matching values. index returns the first matching position and raises ValueError if no match exists in the selected range. reverse changes the order of the existing list in place and returns None. In contrast, values[::-1] creates a reversed copy.
understand.whyItMatters: These methods help inspect repeated values, locate an element and reverse an existing sequence without writing manual loops. Understanding which methods mutate the list prevents accidental data changes.
understand.analogy: count() counts matching labels, index() finds the first numbered position, and reverse() turns the same row of cards around from end to beginning.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not show zero-based indexing, optional search bounds or the difference between in-place mutation and creating a new list.
understand.summary: Use count() for frequency, index() for the first match and reverse() to reverse the original list in place.

explain.narrative:
## count(value)
`items.count(value)` returns the number of times a value appears. It returns zero when there is no match.

## index(value, start, end)
`items.index(value)` returns the first matching zero-based index. Optional start and end arguments restrict the search; the end is excluded. A missing value raises `ValueError`.

## reverse()
`items.reverse()` reverses the existing list in place and returns `None`. Use `items[::-1]` when a new reversed list is needed and the original must remain unchanged.
